mfg1-mechanical-formative-001.stem: A lathe starts vibrating differently from normal. You can operate the stop control from a safe position. What should you do first?
options: Keep machining until the delivery deadline is met.
Stop it using the prescribed procedure and report the abnormal condition to your supervisor.
Hold the moving part by hand to investigate the vibration.
Tell only the person next to you and leave the machine running.
reasons: Putting the deadline first leaves the hazard uncontrolled and can worsen defects.
Ignoring an abnormal condition can lead to an accident. Do not restart without permission; follow workplace instructions.
Touching moving parts creates an entanglement hazard.
Informing someone alone does not remove the dangerous condition. Stop as required and notify the responsible person.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-002.stem: You did not hear the machining instruction clearly and do not know the spindle speed. What is the best way to ask before starting?
options: Guess and use the same speed as for the previous product.
Ask again after the work is finished.
Simply answer, “It is fine.”
Say, “I have not confirmed the spindle speed. Could we check the instruction sheet together?”
reasons: Different products or tools may require different conditions; do not guess.
The check comes too late and machining may already have used unsuitable conditions.
This hides the lack of understanding and does not lead to clarification.
Identify the specific condition that is unclear and confirm it before starting to prevent incorrect operation.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-003.stem: All the required hex keys are available, but you search through the drawer every time. What most directly improves this?
options: Assign and label a location for each size, and return each key there.
Throw away all the keys, including the necessary ones.
Only increase the number of tools.
Change the person responsible for searching every day.
reasons: Arranging necessary items so they are easy to retrieve reduces searching and mix-ups.
Sorting means distinguishing necessary from unnecessary items, not discarding needed tools.
More tools do not solve the problem if their locations remain unclear.
Changing the person does not fix the arrangement.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-004.stem: A shelf rule says to keep four to eight inserts of the same part number. There are only two. Which control is being checked?
options: Fixed location
Fixed item
Fixed quantity
Cleaning
reasons: This specifies where items are stored; the issue here is whether the quantity is within range.
This specifies which item belongs in a location; the question concerns the number, not the part number.
Fixed quantity sets and manages the number stored. Two is below the lower limit of four; follow the replenishment procedure.
Cleaning removes dirt and is different from quantity control.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-005.stem: You are drilling with a drill press. Which statement about gloves is correct?
options: Thin gloves cannot become entangled.
Two layers of leather gloves make drilling safe.
Safety glasses allow you to choose any gloves you like.
Do not wear gloves during drilling, because they can be caught by the rotating cutting tool.
reasons: Thinness does not eliminate the entanglement hazard.
Adding layers does not remove the entanglement hazard.
Eye protection and glove entanglement are separate hazards.
Gloves can become entangled in the drill press. Select protection for the task and also follow the other required safety measures.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-006.stem: You watched an instructor demonstrate a task once, but still cannot explain how to check the setting. What should happen next in on-the-job training?
options: Immediately perform the production task alone because you saw it once.
Ask about what is unclear, explain it back, then practise within the scope checked by the instructor.
Choose an arbitrary setting and show only the result.
Close the instructions without asking.
reasons: This moves to independent work without confirming understanding.
Having seen a task is different from performing it safely. Check understanding and practise within the specified scope under supervision.
Guessing a setting can harm quality and safety.
The uncertainty remains and understanding has not been checked.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-007.stem: After instruction on a tightening setting, which response best helps confirm understanding?
options: Keep saying “yes” even though you do not understand.
Say that everyone else probably understands.
Explain in your own words the display to check, the value and unit, and the conditions requiring a stop.
Remember the number but omit its unit.
reasons: This does not demonstrate specific understanding.
Other people’s understanding does not confirm your own.
Explaining specific check points lets the instructor identify misunderstandings.
The same number can mean different things with different units.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-008.stem: A cart is approaching a corner, and its load obstructs the operator’s view. Which description identifies a specific hazard?
options: Proceeding around the corner without a clear view can cause a collision with a pedestrian in the crossing aisle.
It somehow feels dangerous.
The operator should just try harder.
All carts always cause accidents.
reasons: This links the cause, action and possible accident, making countermeasures easier to discuss.
The cause and type of accident are unclear.
This neither describes the hazard nor gives a concrete countermeasure.
This ignores the conditions and does not analyse the actual situation.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-009.stem: A hazard-prediction discussion ends with “be careful in the aisle.” How can the countermeasure be made specific?
options: Change the wording to “be even more careful.”
Check visibility and traffic routes, then specify where to stop and look according to workplace rules.
Recreate the unsafe transport method to test it.
Discuss the issue but ignore equipment problems.
reasons: Stronger wording alone does not define an action.
Specify what to do, when and where so that the countermeasure can be carried out.
KYT is not training that deliberately creates the actual danger.
Equipment and environmental causes also need consideration.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-010.stem: Oil returns to the same aisle even after cleaning. What is needed to prevent recurrence?
options: Only clean more often without investigating the cause.
Keep walking through until people get used to the oil.
Apply the prescribed temporary controls, request an inspection of the leak’s cause, and check again after corrective action.
Modify the pipe yourself without authorization.
reasons: This removes current contamination but leaves the cause.
This does not reduce the slipping hazard.
Cleaning alone leaves the source of the leak. Address the cause and verify the effectiveness of the action.
An unauthorized change can introduce new hazards.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-011.stem: Which statement is correct after a risk-control measure has been implemented?
options: Check for remaining and newly introduced hazards, and share the findings with everyone concerned.
One control measure always reduces the chance of an accident to zero.
Inspection records are no longer needed.
Do not report a new hazard because the plan has already been approved.
reasons: Failures and changing conditions remain possible, so verify effectiveness and residual risk.
A measure does not necessarily eliminate every hazard completely.
Records help confirm effectiveness and changes.
New hazards also need assessment and a response.

mfg1-mechanical-formative-012.stem: A worker says, “I am wearing safety glasses, so I can remove the machine guard.” Which judgment is correct?
options: Glasses prevent every hazard, not just hazards to the eyes.
A guard is unnecessary if the job is short.
Remove the guard if someone else has removed theirs.
Safety glasses do not replace the guard; the guard and operating procedure must also be followed.
reasons: Eye protection does not protect against every other danger.
A short job still exposes the worker to danger.
Another person’s action does not justify bypassing safety procedures.
Personal protective equipment works together with equipment safeguards, not as a reason to disable them.

mfg1-electrical-formative-001.stem: A stranded wire is marked 1.25 mm², while a tool shows 1.25 mm for solid-wire diameter. How should you choose the tool setting?
options: Use it because both numbers are 1.25.
Distinguish cross-sectional area from diameter and check the wire and tool compatibility tables.
Rewrite mm² as mm.
Ignore wire size because it does not affect quality.
reasons: This confuses different quantities and units.
mm² measures area; mm measures length. The same number does not establish a matching tool setting.
Changing the unit label does not convert the specification.
Compatibility affects conductor damage and connection quality.

mfg1-electrical-formative-002.stem: Some strands are cut after insulation is removed with a wire stripper. What should you do?
options: Conductor damage does not matter if the insulation is removed.
Hide the cut strands by fitting a terminal.
Continue production using another blade whose compatibility is unknown.
Handle the nonconformity according to the work standard and check tool compatibility and processing conditions.
reasons: Conductor scratches and cut strands are also inspection items.
This leaves the damage and obstructs inspection and proper correction.
An unverified tool change does not resolve the cause.
Cut strands and conductor damage must be checked. Removing the insulation alone does not make the result acceptable.

mfg1-electrical-formative-003.stem: You are about to reposition a wire while the solder is solidifying. What protects joint quality?
options: Keep it still during solidification, inspect after cooling, and use an approved rework procedure if needed.
Pull hard before it solidifies; quality will not change.
Inspection after cooling is unnecessary.
Adding more solder fixes every defect.
reasons: Movement during solidification can disturb the joint. Check against the criteria rather than forcing an adjustment.
Movement can affect the joint quality.
The soldered joint must be checked against inspection criteria.
Extra solder does not necessarily correct a poor joint and may create bridging.

mfg1-electrical-formative-004.stem: Solder has joined two adjacent terminals that should not be connected. What condition requires attention?
options: More solder always means a better joint.
A shiny surface means bridging need not be checked.
An unwanted bridge between adjacent parts; handle the nonconformity according to inspection criteria.
The connection state does not matter if the solder material is correct.
reasons: Excess solder can create unintended electrical connections.
One visual feature does not justify ignoring the connection state.
Unwanted solder bridging is an inspection concern and must not be accepted without proper disposition.
Correct material still requires inspection of the finished joint.

mfg1-electrical-formative-005.stem: A drawing specifies a depth measurement. Which part of a caliper is used?
options: Only the closed outside jaws
Clamp the outside surface firmly with the inside jaws.
The length of the handle
The depth bar
reasons: The outside jaws are for external dimensions.
The inside jaws are for internal dimensions; the application and contact are incorrect.
A part not intended for the measurement cannot provide the specified measurement.
Use the depth bar for depth; distinguish the measuring parts and reference surfaces for outside, inside and depth measurements.

mfg1-electrical-formative-006.stem: A caliper has a minimum reading of 0.05 mm. The main scale reads 18 mm and the vernier fraction is 0.45 mm. What is the measurement?
reasons: This adds the minimum reading instead of the actual vernier fraction.
Add the vernier fraction, 0.45 mm, to the main-scale value, 18 mm.
This omits the main-scale value of 18 mm.
This adds the fraction twice.

mfg1-electrical-formative-007.stem: This is a desk calculation. What current flows through an ideal 60 Ω resistor with 12 V applied in a DC circuit?
options: 5 A
reasons: 60 / 12 reverses the required division.
Multiplying 12 by 60 does not give the current.
I = V / R, so 12 / 60 = 0.2 A. This calculation is not an instruction to connect actual equipment.
12 / 60 is 0.2; the decimal point is one place wrong.

mfg1-electrical-formative-008.stem: On a 0.01 mm micrometer, the sleeve shows 4 mm and the following 0.5 mm line; the thimble reads 18. What is the measurement?
reasons: Add 18 × 0.01 = 0.18 mm to the sleeve reading of 4.5 mm: 4.68 mm.
This misses the 0.5 mm line.
A thimble reading of 18 means 0.18 mm; do not concatenate the numbers.
This mixes up the meanings of the sleeve and thimble readings.

mfg1-electrical-formative-009.stem: How should you make the final contact with a micrometer to keep the measuring force consistent?
options: Tightening as hard as possible improves accuracy.
Use that model’s constant-force mechanism according to its instructions.
Have a different person tighten it by feel each time.
Read the scale without placing the object between the measuring faces.
reasons: Excess force can cause error or deformation.
Excessive force can deform the object or instrument; use the prescribed measuring force.
Inconsistent force makes results harder to compare.
This does not measure the object’s dimension.

mfg1-electrical-formative-010.stem: Before measuring the voltage of a training DC circuit, you notice the red lead is still in the current input. What should you do?
options: Switch to the voltage function; any input terminal is acceptable.
Touch both supply terminals briefly to see what happens.
Do not touch the circuit yet; check the input terminal, function, range and connection against the manual and procedure.
Keep changing the leads until a value appears.
reasons: Both the function and the correct input terminal must be checked.
Even a brief contact can cause a short circuit or damage.
Putting a meter in a current-input configuration across a supply can cause a short circuit or damage; check before connecting.
Unplanned changes do not establish safe, suitable connections.

mfg1-electrical-formative-011.stem: What is an appropriate preparation for measuring a resistor in a circuit?
options: Ensure it is de-energized, deal with residual charge and make any required disconnection according to the specified procedure.
Leave the circuit energized and select resistance mode.
Connect the current-input terminal across the supply.
Once the switch is off, stored charge can be ignored.
reasons: Resistance measurement uses the meter’s own power. Switching off alone does not establish that all necessary precautions are complete.
Do not measure resistance on an energized circuit.
This risks a short circuit and is not preparation for resistance measurement.
Charge may remain after the supply is switched off.

mfg1-electrical-formative-012.stem: A training waveform uses 0.5 ms/div and one complete period spans 4 div. What is the frequency?
options: 0.5 Hz
2 Hz
500 Hz
reasons: This results from an incorrect time conversion or treating milliseconds as seconds.
This treats the period’s number as the frequency.
The reciprocal and time conversion do not give this result.
The period is 0.5 × 4 = 2 ms = 0.002 s. Frequency is 1 / 0.002 = 500 Hz.

mfg1-surface-formative-001.stem: In ordinary DC electroplating, metal ions gain electrons and become metal on the workpiece. Which electrode is the workpiece connected to?
options: The anode
The cathode
Any location where no current flows
The liquid temperature alone determines the electrode
reasons: In ordinary electroplating that deposits metal on the workpiece, it is the cathode; do not confuse this with anodizing.
Reduction occurs as metal ions gain electrons on the workpiece, so it is the cathode. Do not apply this relationship unchanged to anodizing.
Electroplating requires a suitable current path and contact for the reaction.
Temperature alone does not determine electrode roles; check the circuit and reaction.

mfg1-surface-formative-002.stem: A chemical container’s label is unreadable and its contents cannot be confirmed. What is the correct approach?
options: Smell it directly to identify it.
Treat liquids of the same colour as the same chemical.
Add a small amount to another liquid without identifying it.
Hold its use and tell the responsible person its location and condition.
reasons: This can expose you to an unknown chemical and is not an appropriate identification method.
Colour alone cannot identify the composition.
Even a small amount can create a reaction or mixing hazard; do not use it without authorization.
Do not identify it by appearance or smell; do not use it until it has been confirmed.

mfg1-surface-formative-003.stem: For a calculation exercise, the total treated area is 3.0 dm² and the current is 12 A. What is the average current density?
options: 4.0 A/dm²
36 A/dm²
0.25 A/dm²
reasons: Average current density is current divided by treated area: 12 / 3.0 = 4.0 A/dm². Use the total area specified. This is not a recommended production setting.
This multiplies current by area; current density requires division.
This divides area by current, reversing the formula.
The number is correct, but a current-density unit must include area in the denominator.

mfg1-surface-formative-004.stem: You plan to use the same thickness meter on two treated parts with different shapes and materials. What must be checked?
options: Both parts are metal, so no suitability check is needed.
More display digits guarantee accurate measurement of every coating.
Whether the method and instrument suit the substrate, coating, layer structure and shape.
Choose whichever meter gives the most favourable result.
reasons: The substrate and coating combination affects which measurement principle is suitable.
Display digits alone do not establish method suitability.
Applicability depends on materials and geometry; being metal parts alone does not establish suitability.
Choose a method that matches the requirement and application, not a preferred result.

mfg1-surface-formative-005.stem: A small hole is found in a coating. What is appropriate?
options: A small hole can never affect corrosion.
Polish without authorization until the hole is invisible, then ship.
Rule out the substrate and earlier processes without checking.
Record its location and condition, identify the part, and support investigation including the substrate and earlier processes.
reasons: Environmental attack can start through a tiny hole.
Hiding the appearance does not establish the cause or acceptance.
There can be several causes; do not exclude them without evidence.
Pinholes can have causes beyond coating formation. Preserve facts instead of hiding the issue through unauthorized rework.

mfg1-surface-formative-006.stem: Corrosion is found where different metals contacted one another. What combination should be checked?
options: Metal names alone determine corrosion rate in every environment.
The contacting metals, the presence of liquid or moisture, damage and storage conditions.
Moisture in packaging has no relationship to metal corrosion.
Wiping away discoloration makes investigation unnecessary.
reasons: Coatings, environment and area relationships also matter.
Dissimilar-metal contact and an electrolyte can contribute to corrosion. Metal names alone do not establish every condition.
Water-based electrolytes can be involved.
Removing a surface change does not identify its cause or the state under the coating.

mfg1-surface-formative-007.stem: A plating bath looks the same as yesterday. Which statement about pH measurement is correct?
options: The same colour always means the same pH.
pH is the number of finished products.
Do not judge by appearance alone; measure using the specified method and frequency.
Skipping measurement stabilizes the bath.
reasons: Colour alone does not establish pH.
pH concerns acidity and alkalinity, not product count.
pH affects coating thickness and appearance. A similar appearance does not prove the value is within range.
Skipping measurement does not stabilize the bath and can hide abnormal conditions.

mfg1-surface-formative-008.stem: Why should the measurement temperature be checked when comparing pH-meter readings?
options: Because pH measurement is affected by temperature.
Temperature makes pH measurement unnecessary.
A pH meter is the same as a thermometer.
Changing temperature never changes measurement conditions.
reasons: Measurement conditions matter when interpreting values. Check and record temperature conditions according to instrument and workplace procedures.
Temperature alone cannot determine pH.
These instruments measure different quantities.
This incorrectly ignores temperature effects.

mfg1-surface-formative-009.stem: The supply display shows the planned value, but poor fixture contact is suspected. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A correct supply display guarantees correct workpiece conditions.
Do not infer the workpiece’s current condition from the display alone; request the prescribed contact and loading checks.
Reverse the wiring during operation without authorization.
Contact has no effect on coating thickness.
reasons: The display alone cannot guarantee local contact or surface condition.
Poor contact can prevent the intended current from reaching the workpiece. Use the specified verification procedure.
This is an unsafe, unauthorized change, not a verification method.
The current path and contact are part of the process conditions.

mfg1-surface-formative-010.stem: Two cases have the same calculated average current density. What is correct about thickness at differently shaped locations?
options: The same average guarantees the same thickness everywhere.
Shape alone precisely determines final thickness in every bath.
Local current distribution can still differ and cause thickness differences.
Always set current to its maximum if thickness is uneven.
reasons: An average does not guarantee identical local distributions.
Bath properties, positioning and agitation also affect the result.
Projections and recesses can have different distributions. Bath properties and positioning also matter; check individual locations.
Excess current can harm appearance and deposition stability.

mfg1-surface-formative-011.stem: Which explanation distinguishes aluminium anodizing from ordinary electroplating?
options: The aluminium workpiece is the anode, and an oxide coating forms at its substrate surface.
The workpiece is the cathode and silver must always be deposited.
A natural oxide film makes every pretreatment unnecessary.
An attractive colour removes the need to check thickness or required properties.
reasons: The workpiece role and coating formation differ from metal deposition at the cathode in ordinary electroplating.
This confuses electroplating with anodizing.
Controlled processing and pretreatment depend on the required quality.
Appearance alone cannot establish corrosion resistance or every other requirement.

mfg1-surface-formative-012.stem: The exercise criterion is 9–15 μm at each specified location. Three readings are 8, 12 and 16 μm; the average is 12 μm. What is correct?
options: Accept all locations because the average is 12 μm.
Delete 8 and 16 μm and record only 12 μm.
Rewrite every location as 12 μm.
Two locations are out of range; do not accept by the average alone. Record and report each location’s value.
reasons: The criterion applies to each location, not the average; two out-of-range results cannot be ignored.
Removing unfavourable data hides the actual condition and prevents traceability and proper judgment.
Recording the average as the measured value at each location is inaccurate.
The criterion applies to each location: 8 is below the minimum and 16 exceeds the maximum. An average of 12 does not cancel these failures. The range is for this exercise.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q01.stem: A container’s hazard label has disappeared and its contents cannot be confirmed. What should you do?
options: Smell it directly.
Do not use it; report its location and condition to the responsible person.
Use it as the same liquid as another of the same colour.
Transfer it to another container and discard the label.
reasons: This risks exposure to an unknown substance.
Do not guess the identity; hold use until it is confirmed.
Colour alone cannot identify a substance.
This loses identification information and can cause mix-ups.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q02.stem: Can a part outside the customer’s specified dimensions be accepted because it looks attractive?
options: Yes. Gloss is the whole of quality.
Yes, if production quantity is high.
Change the drawing without telling the customer.
No. Check appearance and dimensional conformity separately.
reasons: Quality is not determined by appearance alone.
Quantity does not correct dimensional nonconformity.
Unauthorized changes cannot make the part conform to the requirement.
The specified dimensions are also quality acceptance requirements.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q03.stem: Dimensions changed after a tool replacement. What is appropriate in a 4M investigation?
options: Record replacement time, tool specifications and measurements, and compare other 4M changes.
Conclude that the tool replacement must be the cause.
Delete earlier records and stop comparisons.
4M considers only material, so ignore tools.
reasons: Relate actual changes to the problem without prematurely blaming only the tool.
A nearby event in time does not by itself prove causation.
This loses information needed to examine the change.
4M includes people, machines, materials and methods.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q04.stem: The tool specified in the work standard cannot be found. What is appropriate?
options: Use any tool with a similar shape.
Delete the tool name from the standard.
Ask the responsible person instead of choosing a substitute yourself.
Use your hands without checking.
reasons: Shape alone does not establish suitability.
An unauthorized change undermines standard control.
Specified tools are part of the common safety and quality requirements.
The necessary conditions have not been confirmed.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q05.stem: You want to see the shape of a dimensional-data distribution and where most values lie. Which tool is suitable?
options: An employee list
A table containing only process order
A tool loan record
A histogram
reasons: It does not show measured-value distribution.
Sequence alone does not show dimensional distribution.
Tool loans and dimensional distributions are different information.
It shows the distribution and variation of data such as dimensions.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q06.stem: A drawing length is 0.025 m. What is this in millimetres?
options: 25 mm
250 mm
reasons: The unit was changed without conversion.
This is ten times too large.
This is one hundred times too large.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q07.stem: Three of 100 inspected products are nonconforming. What is the percentage of nonconforming products?
reasons: Three out of 100 is not 30%.
The ratio 0.03 has not been converted to a percentage.
3 / 100 × 100 = 3%. Use the number of nonconforming products.
This is the percentage of the 97 conforming products.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q08.stem: Someone proposes omitting a specified inspection to reduce production cost. What is appropriate quality management?
options: Maintain required quality and safety, and consider cost improvements through approved methods.
Lower cost permits ignoring quality requirements.
Inspection results are unnecessary if the deadline is met.
Do not record quality issues until the customer uses the product.
reasons: Cost alone must not take priority over conformity.
Cost reduction does not justify nonconformity.
Delivery timing and inspection requirements are separate conditions.
This obstructs early checking and recording.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q09.stem: The mean dimension equals the target. Can you conclude that every product is within specification?
options: Yes. The mean is the dimension of every product.
No. Check individual values and variation too.
Yes. Variation no longer exists.
Delete individual out-of-specification values.
reasons: A mean is not identical to each individual value.
The mean alone cannot establish whether any product is out of specification.
The distribution can still be wide even when its mean meets the target.
Deleting unfavourable data hides the actual condition.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q10.stem: You want to check a process’s control items and measurement methods in a QC process chart. What should you do?
options: Read only the process name and ignore control items.
Use another product’s chart unconditionally.
Match the target process to its applicable control conditions and methods.
Rewrite an unclear control value yourself.
reasons: This does not verify the control content.
Its scope may be different.
Check what is controlled and how at each process.
This is an unauthorized change to control conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q11.stem: You want to plot points to investigate the relationship between two measured quantities. Which tool is suitable?
options: A scatter plot
A histogram
A work-sequence instruction
An attendance sheet
reasons: It shows two variables using horizontal and vertical axes.
A histogram is used to examine the distribution of one quantity.
It is not a plot of two variables.
It does not show the relationship between the measured quantities.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-02-q12.stem: Which inspection judges a lot by inspecting only part of it?
options: 100% inspection
The same as no inspection
Inspection of only whichever good items you prefer
Sampling inspection
reasons: This examines every item.
Inspecting a sample differs from inspecting nothing.
Sampling requires a prescribed selection method and criteria.
A specified selection method and criteria are used to judge the lot.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q01.stem: What properties are primarily examined in a tensile test?
options: Surface colour alone
The acidity of a liquid
Supply frequency
Strength and elongation under a pulling load.
reasons: This is not a test only of colour.
Tensile testing differs from pH measurement.
This is not the measured subject of a tensile test.
Tensile load and deformation are used to assess mechanical properties.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q02.stem: You want to investigate internal defects without cutting the finished product. Which category fits?
options: Non-destructive testing
Destructive testing that always cuts it
Guessing without inspecting appearance
Discarding every product to investigate
reasons: It investigates defects without destroying the object.
This conflicts with the no-cutting condition.
This is an unverified judgment, not inspection.
This does not describe the inspection needed.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q03.stem: What problem can arise if chips remain on a measuring face?
options: There is no effect between metal surfaces.
More display digits automatically compensate for chips.
The foreign material’s thickness can affect the result.
Clamping harder always makes the result accurate.
reasons: Foreign material can affect measurement even if the material is similar.
Display resolution does not automatically remove dirt.
Clean and check the instrument and object before measurement.
Excess force can cause deformation or error.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q04.stem: Which caliper part is used to measure a hole’s internal diameter?
options: Only the outside jaws
The depth bar
An unmarked handle
The inside jaws
reasons: These are intended for external dimensions.
This measures depth.
This is not the intended reference measuring part.
Use the measuring part for internal dimensions.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q05.stem: A 0.01 mm micrometer reads 7.5 mm on the sleeve and 26 on the thimble. What is the value?
reasons: The 0.5 mm portion was missed.
Add quantities in matching units; do not concatenate numbers.
The sleeve and thimble readings have been confused.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q06.stem: A drawing is at scale 1:2 and has a dimension marked 60 mm. What is the actual dimension?
options: 30 mm
120 mm
60 mm
It cannot be known without measuring the drawing.
reasons: This applies the scale again to the dimension annotation.
This double-converts the annotation in the opposite direction.
A dimension annotation gives the actual value, not the apparent drawn length.
Read the actual dimension from the annotation.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q07.stem: A dimension is 10.00 ± 0.05 mm and the measurement is 10.06 mm. Under a simple limit comparison, what is the result?
options: It is within range.
It is below the lower limit.
Round it to 10.00 without authorization to accept it.
It exceeds the upper limit of 10.05 mm.
reasons: 10.06 is greater than 10.05.
It is greater than the lower limit of 9.95.
Do not round to conceal an out-of-specification result.
The range is 9.95–10.05 mm, so 10.06 is above it.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q08.stem: Can hardness alone determine all tensile properties and suitability for every use?
options: Yes. All mechanical properties are the same value.
No. Check the test method and required properties.
Higher hardness is best for every use.
Differences in test method need not be recorded.
reasons: Different properties cannot be treated as one value.
Do not confuse hardness with other properties; use tests suited to the requirement.
The particular application and conditions must be considered.
Methods and conditions are needed for meaningful comparisons.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q09.stem: Sensory inspection results differ between inspectors. What is appropriate?
options: Align reference samples, acceptance criteria and conditions such as lighting.
Use only the experienced inspector’s preference.
Delete only the rejection records.
Inspection conditions do not affect quality.
reasons: Even sensory inspection needs clear criteria and conditions to reduce variation.
This is not a common acceptance criterion.
This conceals the reason for differing judgments.
Conditions such as lighting can affect judgment.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q10.stem: Can a recently heated part be compared directly with a room-temperature part in precision measurement?
options: Temperature never affects length.
A hotter part always has the correct dimension.
Consider temperature effects and check the specified measurement conditions.
Grip it firmly to adjust its temperature by feel.
reasons: This ignores thermal dimensional change.
Accuracy is not determined by being hotter.
Temperature differences can alter dimensions; align the conditions.
This does not confirm specified conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q11.stem: A caliper was applied at an angle and the reading is near a specification limit. What should you do?
options: Check contact and instrument condition, then measure using the specified method.
Accept without checking because it is close.
Record only the smallest value.
Change the drawing limit.
reasons: Angled contact can cause error; do not accept merely because the result is convenient.
The unsuitable measurement condition remains.
Selected values alone do not represent the actual condition.
Do not change the requirement without authorization.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-03-q12.stem: What is a dimensional tolerance width?
options: The amount by which records may be freely rewritten
The difference between the maximum and minimum permitted dimensions.
The paper margin when printing the drawing
One fixed value for every product
reasons: Tolerance does not authorize changing records.
Tolerance width is the maximum permitted size minus the minimum; distinguish it from a deviation relative to nominal size.
Paper margins differ from product requirements.
Tolerances are specified according to each requirement.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q01.stem: An assembled product may be nonconforming. How should it initially be handled?
options: Mix it with good products and ship it.
Identify it, separate it from good products, and record and report the findings.
Put it out of sight without a record.
Change the inspection value to a passing value.
reasons: This risks releasing a nonconforming product.
Prevent mixing and preserve traceable information.
Its status and location become untraceable.
Records must not be falsified.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q02.stem: You find a bent terminal during board inspection. Which report is useful?
options: Assert that someone handled it roughly.
Say only, “Something is strange.”
Wait until the next working day to report it.
State the product, discovery time, observed condition and action already taken.
reasons: This confuses an unconfirmed cause with fact.
The product and condition are not specific.
Delayed action may allow the impact to spread.
Facts and actions support decisions and traceability.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q03.stem: How should hazard-prediction activities continue after a control is implemented?
options: Check effectiveness and share remaining or new hazards.
Assume the chance of an accident is zero.
Discard all records.
Ignore new hazards because they were outside the plan.
reasons: Implementation alone does not establish effectiveness or residual risk.
A measure does not necessarily remove every hazard.
This loses information needed for review.
Changes in the situation must also be checked.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q04.stem: A dimension is outside product specification but inside a control chart’s control limits. How should shipment be judged?
options: Any value inside control limits can always be shipped, even outside specification.
Control limits and specification limits are always identical.
Do not accept only because it is within control limits; handle it according to product specifications.
Rewrite the out-of-specification measurement to a control-limit value.
reasons: This confuses process monitoring with product requirements.
Their purposes and how they are established differ.
Control limits monitor the process; specification limits judge product conformity. Their purposes differ.
Measured values must not be altered.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q05.stem: Which chart shows defect categories in descending frequency together with cumulative percentage?
options: A circuit connection diagram
A component layout drawing
An attendance sheet
A Pareto chart
reasons: It shows electrical connections.
It shows positions, not defect-count analysis.
It does not show defect categories and cumulative percentage.
It combines descending-frequency bars and cumulative percentage.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q06.stem: A drawing uses a dashed line. How should its meaning be determined?
options: Treat every line as a cutting position.
Check the line type and drawing rules, including whether it represents a hidden feature.
Ignore every thin line.
Prefer screen length over the dimension annotation.
reasons: This ignores different line meanings.
Line types have meanings and must not all be treated as solid lines.
Line weight and type also carry information.
Actual dimensions are read from annotations.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q07.stem: You want to confirm physical component mounting positions. Which drawing is most useful first?
options: A diagram showing connections only
A delivery schedule
A layout drawing
A temperature-history graph
reasons: Connection information and physical position are not identical.
It does not show mounting positions.
It shows the physical arrangement of equipment or components.
It does not show component layout.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q08.stem: You did not hear a terminal number in a work instruction. What should you do before starting?
options: Connect to any empty terminal.
Pretend you confirmed it.
Think about the number only after finishing.
Ask for the number again and check the target to confirm understanding.
reasons: This does not guarantee the specified connection.
The uncertainty remains.
This checks too late.
Guessing terminal numbers can cause incorrect connections.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q09.stem: KYT identifies an equipment hazard. What approach is appropriate?
options: A loud warning always makes equipment controls unnecessary.
Do not rely only on warnings; discuss equipment and process controls that reduce the hazard.
Modify the safety device yourself without authorization.
No hazard exists if only experienced people work.
reasons: This does not sufficiently consider reducing the hazard itself.
Attention alone may leave the cause unchanged.
An unauthorized change can create new hazards.
Experience alone does not remove equipment hazards.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q10.stem: What is primarily examined with a histogram?
options: The distribution and variation of measured data.
Component wiring order
Only personal work schedules
A culprit established without investigation
reasons: It shows where values occur and how often.
That is information for circuit diagrams and related drawings.
These differ from dimensional-data distributions.
A distribution alone does not prove cause or responsibility.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q11.stem: You selected the most frequent defect category. What should be considered next?
options: Ignore even serious hazards if they occur rarely.
The most frequent defect is always caused by the operator.
Also consider safety severity and causes when planning improvement.
Improvement is complete if you reduce recorded counts.
reasons: Low frequency does not cancel severity.
Counts alone cannot establish a cause.
Frequency alone must not push serious hazards aside.
Changing records is not actual improvement.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-02-q12.stem: Two components connected in a connection diagram appear far apart in a layout drawing. How should this be understood?
options: Electrical connection and physical location differ; distinguish each drawing’s purpose.
Adjacent symbols must be physically adjacent.
Distant components cannot be electrically connected.
Rewrite either drawing without authorization.
reasons: Diagram proximity or line length alone does not establish actual distance.
This confuses logical connection with actual layout.
Wires can connect equipment at different locations.
Do not change drawings without understanding their purposes.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q01.stem: Which explanation distinguishes conductors from insulators?
options: Conductors and insulators have identical uses.
Any insulator is safe at every voltage.
Colour alone determines electrical properties.
Conductors provide current paths; insulators help prevent unwanted current paths.
reasons: Their ease of conducting current differs.
Operating conditions and voltage withstand must be checked.
Appearance alone cannot establish material specifications.
Select materials for the required electrical properties and conditions.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q02.stem: What is the range of a 1.0 kΩ resistor with ±5% tolerance?
options: Exactly 1000 Ω only
reasons: 1000 × 0.05 = 50 Ω, so the range is 1000 ± 50 Ω.
This corresponds to ±0.5%, not ±5%.
This corresponds to ±50%.
This ignores the tolerance.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q03.stem: Ideal 20 Ω and 30 Ω resistors are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
reasons: This is their parallel equivalent.
Multiplying alone does not give series resistance.
Series resistances add: 20 + 30 = 50.
Use the sum, not the difference.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q04.stem: What is the basic explanation of diode rectification?
options: Exactly the same current flows in either direction.
It always causes mechanical movement.
Polarity markings need not be checked.
It uses the property of conducting more readily in one direction than the other.
reasons: This ignores directional properties.
This does not describe rectification.
Mounting direction must be confirmed.
The difference in current flow with direction is used.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q05.stem: What should be checked in packaging for a static-sensitive IC?
options: Whether the specified antistatic or other packaging meets the part’s handling requirements.
All transparent bags offer the same protection.
Small components are unaffected by static electricity.
Dry hands make packaging unnecessary.
reasons: Do not assume every ordinary bag is equivalent.
Transparency does not guarantee ESD protection.
Size alone does not determine immunity.
Hand condition alone does not establish ESD protection.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q06.stem: A training lamp lights only when both switches A and B are ON. Which logic is this?
options: OR
Always ON
AND
Control that ignores both A and B
reasons: OR can be true when either input is true.
This does not use input conditions.
The output occurs when both conditions are true.
This does not match the stated condition.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q07.stem: Which activity schedules checks and replacement before a failure occurs?
options: Corrective maintenance after failure
Preventive maintenance
Hiding inspection records
Only waiting for failure
reasons: This responds after failure.
Condition checks and servicing are performed in advance to prevent failures.
This loses maintenance information.
This is not preventive action.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q08.stem: Besides high resistance, what should be checked when selecting an insulating material?
options: The same material name means specifications need not be checked.
Similar appearance means identical ratings.
A low price makes it suitable for every use.
Suitability for required conditions such as temperature and environment.
reasons: Similar material families may have different specifications and uses.
Appearance alone cannot establish ratings.
Price does not guarantee required performance.
Selection must match operating conditions as well as electrical properties.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q09.stem: How should a resistor’s marked and measured values be compared?
options: Any digit difference always means nonconformity.
Check the unit, tolerance and measurement conditions before judging.
Compare the numbers in kΩ and Ω without conversion.
Rewrite the measured value to match the marking.
reasons: A difference within tolerance may be acceptable.
A small difference is not enough to judge; compare against the specified range and conditions.
Comparisons with unmatched units are incorrect.
Changing the record is not judgment.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q10.stem: Two identical ideal resistors are connected in parallel. Compared with one resistor, what is their equivalent resistance?
options: Double
Unchanged
Half
Always zero
reasons: Double applies to two equal resistors in series.
This ignores the added parallel path.
Two equal current paths give an equivalent resistance of R/2.
Two finite parallel resistors do not give zero.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q11.stem: A diode’s polarity marking is unreadable before assembly. What should you do?
options: Check the specification and marking; hold installation if uncertain.
Fit it either way because both directions are the same.
Energize it and select whichever way does not break it.
Scrape away the marking to make it clearer.
reasons: Direction matters, so do not guess.
This ignores directional properties.
Unplanned testing can damage components or equipment.
This removes identification information.

mfg1-electrical-weekly-03-q12.stem: Equipment has been repaired after a failure. What should maintenance records retain?
options: Only the repairer’s impressions
The failure condition, actions and verification results needed to examine recurrence.
Delete inconvenient failure history.
Verification results are unnecessary once it restarts.
reasons: Concrete conditions and actions are difficult to trace.
History supports later inspection and recurrence prevention.
This loses information needed for recurrence analysis.
Safety and function checks and records cannot be omitted.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q01.stem: A buffing tool is pressed against the same spot for a long time. What needs attention?
options: More pressure always improves quality.
Check effects on heat, scratches and shape.
Heat is unrelated to polishing.
Do not record scratches between processes.
reasons: Excess force or time can have harmful effects.
Polishing conditions can change the surface and shape.
Frictional heat must be considered.
This makes causes harder to trace.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q02.stem: What should be checked when using a specific-gravity/concentration relationship to control a bath?
options: The same specific gravity means the same concentration in every liquid.
A scale reads identically from every angle.
Specific gravity alone identifies every individual component.
The relationship applicable to that liquid, and the measurement temperature and method.
reasons: Composition and conditions can change the relationship.
Reading method can introduce error.
It cannot establish the entire composition.
Do not apply another liquid’s relationship or conditions unconditionally.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q03.stem: In a calculation where HCl and NaOH react 1:1, 20 mL of 0.10 mol/L NaOH is used. How many moles of HCl reacted?
options: 2.0 mol
reasons: 20 mL = 0.020 L; 0.10 × 0.020 = 0.0020 mol. The 1:1 ratio gives the same HCl amount.
Millilitres were not converted to litres.
This is ten times too large.
This is one tenth of the correct value.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q04.stem: Which explanation distinguishes g/L mass concentration from mol/L amount concentration?
options: Only the unit names differ; numbers are always identical.
g/L indicates only the solution temperature.
The first is mass per solution volume; the second is amount of substance per solution volume.
mol/L indicates finished-product count.
reasons: Conversion requires information such as molar mass.
It is a unit of mass concentration.
The volume basis is the same, but the numerator and unit differ.
It expresses amount of substance per solution volume.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q05.stem: What is the basic reaction partner of an acidic oxide?
options: It is defined as reacting only with acids.
The name means all such oxides dissolve in water equally fast.
It must be an elemental metal.
It reacts with a base to form a salt.
reasons: This reverses acidic- and basic-oxide descriptions.
Classification alone does not establish dissolution rate.
An oxide differs from a metal element.
This reflects the acidic-oxide/base relationship and the official erratum.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q06.stem: Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ in solution react to form AgCl. What is the appearance of a solid called?
options: Precipitation
Evaporation in which everything becomes gas
A reaction that only dissolves a metal
Conversion of temperature units
reasons: A poorly soluble substance appears as a solid in solution.
Solid formation differs from evaporation.
This reaction produces a solid, poorly soluble salt.
This does not describe a chemical reaction.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q07.stem: Aluminium has density 2.7 g/cm³ and volume 5.0 cm³. What is its mass?
options: 13.5 cm³
reasons: This divides density by volume.
This adds density and volume.
Mass = density × volume, so 2.7 × 5.0 = 13.5.
The resulting mass unit is grams.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q08.stem: A recorded bath temperature differs substantially from yesterday. What should be checked?
options: Record yesterday’s more convenient value.
Check the location, instrument, reading and actual process changes; record and report.
Discard the measurement because the liquid looks unchanged.
Add a large quantity of chemicals before investigating.
reasons: Do not alter measured facts.
Distinguish measurement-condition differences from real process changes.
Appearance alone does not establish temperature.
Unauthorized adjustment is hazardous and leaves the cause unknown.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q09.stem: What is a standard solution used in neutralization titration?
options: Waste liquid of unknown concentration
The darkest-coloured liquid
Any water is equivalent
A solution of known concentration.
reasons: It lacks the known concentration needed for calculation.
Colour intensity does not define a standard solution.
Suitable composition and known concentration are required.
A known concentration is the reference for determining an unknown concentration.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q10.stem: A calculation gives solute molar mass 50 g/mol and mass concentration 100 g/L. What is the molar concentration?
options: 5000 mol/L
2.0 mol/L
0.5 mol/L
100 mol/L
reasons: Divide by molar mass rather than multiply.
100 g/L divided by 50 g/mol equals 2.0 mol/L.
The division order is reversed.
The difference between grams and moles has not been converted.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q11.stem: What is the basic description of an amphoteric oxide?
options: It never reacts with either acids or bases.
It is just another name for an acidic oxide.
It can react with both acids and bases under suitable conditions.
It always reacts at the same rate under every condition.
reasons: This is the opposite of amphoteric behaviour.
The classifications have different meanings.
The classification indicates reactivity toward both.
Classification does not imply a universal reaction rate.

mfg1-surface-weekly-02-q12.stem: To calculate volume in cm³, how should a length of 20 mm be converted?
options: 2.0 cm
20 cm
200 cm
reasons: The length unit has not been converted.
This is ten times too small.
The conversion direction is reversed.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q01.stem: What are the principal metals in brass?
options: Copper and tin
Copper and nickel
Aluminium only
Copper and zinc
reasons: This is the basic combination for bronze.
This is the basic combination for cupronickel.
This does not describe brass.
Brass is primarily a Cu–Zn alloy.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q02.stem: Can degreasing and activation be treated as the same process?
options: No. Removing oil and activating the surface serve different purposes.
Yes. All use the same liquid and treatment.
Oil always disappears later, so degreasing is unnecessary.
Workers may freely change their order.
reasons: Check each pretreatment’s role and sequence.
This confuses different roles and conditions.
Remaining oil can affect quality.
The approved process sequence must be followed.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q03.stem: Blistering is found in a plated coating. What is an appropriate approach to its cause?
options: Flatten it without authorization and ship.
Record location and conditions and investigate several factors, including pretreatment.
All causes are identical, so do not record it.
Mix it with conforming products.
reasons: Hiding the appearance does not establish cause or conformity.
Do not immediately select a single cause from appearance alone.
Different contributing factors can be missed.
This risks releasing a nonconforming product.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q04.stem: Moisture may remain on a part before hot-dip coating. What should be done?
options: Immerse it because the molten metal is hot.
A small amount of water is always safe.
Move your face close to check for splashing.
Do not immerse it; confirm drying and the prescribed procedure with the responsible person.
reasons: This ignores rapid-vaporization hazards.
Quantity alone cannot establish safety.
This approaches the hazard and is not an appropriate check.
Moisture can cause rapid vaporization and splashing.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q05.stem: Which statement about electroless plating is correct?
options: The workpiece must always be a cathode on a DC supply.
No bath control is needed.
Distinguish it from electroplating that supplies current to the workpiece from an external source.
Only the names differ; every principle is identical.
reasons: This describes ordinary electroplating.
Chemical-reaction processes also require condition control.
It uses chemical reactions and is not identical to ordinary electroplating.
This ignores differences in principles and conditions.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q06.stem: Can clear wastewater be discharged untreated?
options: No. It may contain harmful dissolved components even when clear.
Yes. Clear means every component is safe.
Measuring pH reveals every metal concentration.
Mixing unknown liquids makes them safe.
reasons: Appearance alone cannot establish safety or compliance.
Dissolved substances may be invisible.
pH and metal concentration are different information.
Mixing can cause hazardous reactions.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q07.stem: Noise from an exhaust system is bothersome. What is appropriate?
options: Stop it without permission until the noise disappears.
Unobtrusive sound always proves proper extraction.
Do not switch it off without authorization; discuss both safety and noise control with the responsible person.
No complaints means no inspection is needed.
reasons: This can undermine control of harmful emissions.
Sound alone does not guarantee performance.
Noise reduction must not remove necessary exhaust protection.
Complaints and functional inspection are separate issues.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q08.stem: Which basic compositions distinguish cupronickel from bronze?
options: Cupronickel is copper–tin; bronze is copper–nickel.
Both consist only of iron.
Only the names differ; the main elements are always identical.
Cupronickel is mainly copper–nickel; bronze is mainly copper–tin.
reasons: The two combinations are reversed.
These are copper alloys, not pure iron.
This ignores compositional differences.
Match each alloy name to its principal elements.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q09.stem: Oil residue is found after pretreatment. What is appropriate?
options: Continue because the next process will certainly fix it.
Identify the affected items, report and confirm approved action.
Increase chemical concentration without authorization.
Delete the oil observation from inspection records.
reasons: This carries an unverified oil-related problem forward.
Handle the pretreatment abnormality rather than hide it in later processing.
This changes safety- and quality-critical conditions without approval.
This loses information needed to trace the cause.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q10.stem: An unplated area is found. Which record is useful?
options: Only “it was defective”
Write “the operator caused it” without verification.
Location, lot, processing conditions, and contact and pretreatment conditions.
Mix it with good parts and forget its location.
reasons: Missing locations and conditions impede investigation.
This confuses speculation with fact.
Comparable facts support cause investigation.
Identification and traceability are lost.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q11.stem: Which description of hot-dip coating is appropriate?
options: It uses molten metal, so high temperature and moisture carry-in hazards require control.
It uses only room-temperature water.
High temperature makes protective equipment and procedures unnecessary.
Textbook values can be applied unchanged to every installation.
reasons: Connect the process principle with its specific hazards.
This differs from the molten-metal principle.
High temperatures require appropriate controls.
Real conditions must follow the equipment and approved procedures.

mfg1-surface-weekly-03-q12.stem: What is appropriate when recording a factory’s environmental effects?
options: Clear wastewater means every environmental impact is zero.
Check relevant effects including gases and noise, not only wastewater.
Treatment equipment cannot create environmental effects.
Do not record unfavourable measurements.
reasons: Neither appearance nor one item guarantees all effects.
Surface-treatment environmental effects are not limited to one category.
Equipment noise and other effects also need checking.
This obstructs understanding and improvement.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q01.stem: The pre-start daily inspection found no abnormality. May the scheduled periodic inspection be omitted?
options: Yes. They merely repeat exactly the same checks.
No. Daily and periodic inspections have different scopes and purposes.
New equipment never needs inspection.
Skip every check only on busy days.
reasons: Their scopes and methods differ.
Periodic inspection examines details that daily checks may not reveal.
Use and ageing can change its condition.
Production workload does not justify omitting inspections.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q02.stem: A change of shape remains after the force is removed. Which property is involved?
options: Elasticity alone
Electrical conductivity
Melting point
Plasticity
reasons: Elastic deformation returns when the force is removed.
This concerns how readily electricity passes.
This is the temperature at which a solid melts.
Plastic deformation remains after unloading.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q03.stem: Which explanation distinguishes quenching from tempering?
options: Quenching hardens the material; subsequent tempering adjusts hardness and toughness, among other properties.
Tempering always melts the entire metal.
Only the names differ; the conditions are identical.
High hardness makes toughness irrelevant.
reasons: Their objectives and cooling conditions differ even though both involve heating.
It is not an operation that completely melts the metal.
Distinguish their objectives and conditions.
Several properties required for the application must be checked.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q04.stem: What is a basic difference between turning and milling?
options: Both melt material and pour it into a mould.
The milling tool never moves.
Turning mainly rotates the workpiece; milling mainly rotates the cutting tool.
A lathe always thins sheet between rolls.
reasons: That describes casting, not cutting.
It machines through movements including tool rotation.
Distinguish which element rotates to cut the material.
This confuses rolling with turning.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q05.stem: What mainly removes material during grinding?
options: Only paint drying removes material.
Waiting for the material to evaporate naturally.
Unlike cutting, dimensions never change.
Many abrasive grains in a wheel act as small cutting edges.
reasons: This confuses painting and grinding.
This is not the grinding removal principle.
Grinding also removes material and changes dimensions.
Understand machining with abrasive grains rather than only a single cutting edge.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q06.stem: Which process pours molten metal into a mould and solidifies it to form a shape?
options: Forging
Casting
Turning
Rolling
reasons: This mainly deforms metal by applying force.
Metal is melted and solidified in a mould.
A tool cuts a rotating workpiece.
Material is deformed between rolls.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q07.stem: A part meets drawing dimensions but its sliding surface is rough. How should it be assessed?
options: Correct dimensions always guarantee acceptable roughness.
A shiny appearance removes the need for roughness values.
Check dimensional conformity and surface-roughness requirements separately.
Change the dimension and delete the roughness record.
reasons: This merges separate requirements.
Gloss alone does not guarantee specified roughness.
Roughness affects friction and function; dimensions cannot substitute for it.
Requirements must not be changed without authorization.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q08.stem: May an iron part be replaced with aluminium solely because it is lighter at the same volume?
options: Also check strength, deformation, temperature conditions and design approval.
Lower weight always improves every function.
Equal volume always means equal mass regardless of material.
Similar appearance makes material records unnecessary.
reasons: Density-based weight reduction differs from meeting every required part property.
One advantage does not establish all requirements.
Mass depends on density and volume.
Material identity and conformity must be confirmed.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q09.stem: Parts have the same material designation but different heat-treatment histories. How should they be handled?
options: Discard history because the material names match.
Check the treatment and condition against the required properties.
Identical appearance always means identical hardness.
Reheat them arbitrarily if any difference exists.
reasons: This loses the ability to check property differences.
Heat treatment changes structure and properties; the material name alone is insufficient.
Appearance alone does not establish heat-treatment effects.
Do not change heat-treatment conditions without an approved procedure.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q10.stem: Tool wear has changed dimensions or the machined surface. What is appropriate?
options: Ignore wear and increase feed without limit.
Do not inspect the defective surface.
Check the tool and machining results, then follow replacement and adjustment procedures.
A tool maintains identical performance forever if it still cuts.
reasons: Unauthorized changes can worsen the problem.
The impact cannot be established.
Wear affects the finish; do not compensate by blindly continuing.
Tool condition changes with use.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q11.stem: When selecting grinding or polishing, what matters besides the process name?
options: The material, required dimensions and surface condition, and applicable conditions.
Use identical wheels and conditions for every material.
Tool colour alone determines the finish.
Polishing makes every inspection unnecessary.
reasons: Select a method suited to the purpose and material.
Suitability depends on material and application.
Colour alone cannot establish suitability.
Confirm conformity after processing.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-04-q12.stem: The drawing specifies Ra, but the inspection record gives only Rz. Can the numbers be directly compared?
options: Yes. Matching units eliminate any parameter difference.
Use whichever number is smaller.
Simply relabel the result as Ra.
No. Obtain results using the specified index and conditions.
reasons: Different quantities can share a unit but have different definitions.
A convenient selection does not demonstrate conformity.
Do not alter the parameter actually measured.
Ra and Rz are different roughness parameters; do not directly compare numbers alone.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-05-q01.stem: In an ideal resistor circuit at fixed voltage, only the resistance decreases. What happens to current?
options: It decreases.
It must remain unchanged.
Its direction must reverse.
It increases.
reasons: This reverses the effect of a smaller denominator.
This ignores the resistance change.
A resistance decrease alone does not reverse polarity.
I = V/R, so lower resistance at fixed voltage gives higher current.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-05-q02.stem: Which process forms a hollow container by inflating it with air?
options: Blow moulding
Turning that simply cuts metal
Metal rolling
Painting
reasons: Air presses the material against a mould to make hollow products.
This does not describe hollow plastic moulding.
This thins material between rolls.
This forms a coating on a surface.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-05-q03.stem: Besides appearance, what is an important purpose of painting?
options: It always turns the substrate into a different metal.
It makes every dimensional inspection unnecessary.
Protecting the surface against corrosion and similar effects.
It automatically removes all oil underneath.
reasons: Painting does not change the substrate into another metal.
Required inspections remain after painting.
A paint film provides protection as well as appearance.
Surface condition and pretreatment must be checked.

mfg1-mechanical-weekly-05-q04.stem: Packaging protects a product from scratches, but its label has another part number. What is correct?
options: Any label is acceptable if protection is adequate.
Erasing labels makes the package suitable for every product.
Heavy products need no part numbers.
Both protection and information are required; verify the part-number label.
reasons: This can cause shipment and handling errors.
